71.title: The brothers come for bread (Genesis 42)
71.hook: they bow to a man they don't recognize
71.carry: you don't see who it is
71.howItsDone: Jewish commentators read this chapter as the start of the brothers' repair, the moment they admit aloud what they did to Joseph.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner put in charge of Egypt's grain. Your line was store in the good years. Now the lean years arrive.

The famine spreads past Egypt, all the way to Canaan, to Jacob's tents. Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt. Why are you staring at each other? he asks his sons. Go down and buy us food, so we can live. Ten brothers go. Not Benjamin; Jacob won't let Rachel's last son out of his sight. So ten men walk into Egypt with money in their bags and stand before the governor who sells the grain to everyone. And they bow down to him, faces to the ground. Just like the sheaves in the dream they once hated him for.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, NOT BENJAMIN.` → `FACES TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The Torah puts the whole scene in one line: "And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not." How could they miss him? He was seventeen when they sold him; now he's a grown man, shaved and dressed like an Egyptian, speaking through an interpreter. An old explanation, passed on by Rashi, puts it simply: when they sold him he had no beard, and now he had one. But there's a deeper reason. They weren't looking for him. You don't see who it is when you've decided who it can't be. Joseph remembers the dreams. He speaks to them harshly. The Hebrew is clever here: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger to them, two verbs from the same root. He calls them spies. They protest: we are twelve brothers, sons of one man; the youngest is with our father, and one is no more. One is no more. They're talking about him, to his face. Joseph keeps one brother, Simeon, as a hostage: bring me your youngest brother. Then, thinking the governor can't understand Hebrew, the brothers say to each other: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother." We saw his distress when he pleaded with us, and we wouldn't listen. Reuben says, didn't I tell you? And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away and weeps. All these years later, the brothers are finally talking about what they did, and the man they did it to is standing right there, listening.

72.title: The silver cup (Genesis 44:1–17)
72.hook: the test: will the brothers abandon another favorite son?
72.howItsDone: Jews call turning around teshuvah; Maimonides' test for it, facing the same situation and choosing differently, is one way teachers read this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon stayed behind as a hostage in Egypt. Your line was you don't see who it is.

The grain runs out, and the brothers have to go back to Egypt. This time they bring Benjamin, because the governor demanded it. Jacob lets him go only after Judah promises: I'll be responsible for him. If I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. In Egypt, the governor invites them to a feast. Simeon is released. Benjamin gets five times as much food as anyone else: the favorite son, again, getting more, in front of the others. And the brothers seem fine with it. They eat, drink and relax. Next morning they head for home, sacks full.
screen: `THEY BRING BENJAMIN.` → `FIVE TIMES AS MUCH FOR HIM.` → `SACKS FULL, HEADING HOME.`

segments.voice: Before they leave, Joseph gives his steward an order: put my silver cup in the youngest one's sack. They're barely out of the city when the steward catches up. Why have you repaid good with evil? You stole my master's cup! The brothers are so sure of themselves they make a reckless offer: whoever has it, let him die, and the rest of us will be slaves. The steward searches, oldest to youngest. It's in Benjamin's. The brothers tear their clothes, as Jacob did over Joseph's coat, and every one of them turns back to the city. Nobody has to go back. Judah speaks for all of them: "God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants." He doesn't argue about the cup. He's thinking of an older guilt. We'll all be your slaves, he says. Then the governor makes them an easy offer: only the one who had the cup will be my slave; the rest of you, go home in peace. It's the pit all over again. A favored son of Rachel. A chance to be rid of him, and to tell their father something sad but blameless. Not one of them walks away. Maimonides, the great medieval teacher, describes complete repentance, teshuvah, this way: you find yourself in the same situation, with the same pull and the same chance, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't, but because you've changed. The silver cup is that test. Years ago these brothers sold a favorite son. This time they won't.

73.title: Judah's plea (Genesis 44:18–34)
73.hook: Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place
73.howItsDone: Judah's plea opens the weekly Torah portion Vayigash, read in synagogue each winter, and rabbinic teaching remembers Judah as a man who owned his wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvah: the same chance to abandon a favorite son, and the brothers refused. Your line was not this time.

The room is silent. The governor of Egypt has just said: the one with the cup stays as my slave; the rest of you, go. The brothers are on the floor. Benjamin stands there, the cup found in his bag, his whole life about to be taken away. And the Torah says: "Then Judah came near unto him." In Hebrew it's one word, vayigash: and he drew near. Nobody tells him to. Nobody expects him to. Judah, who years ago looked at another brother in a pit and said, let's sell him, walks up to the man who holds all their lives.
screen: `THE ONE WITH THE CUP STAYS.` → `THEN JUDAH CAME NEAR.` → `THE BROTHER WHO SAID SELL HIM.`

segments.voice: Judah's speech isn't clever. It's a story. He tells the governor about their old father, and the son of his old age, whose brother is dead, the only one left from his mother, whom his father loves. He quotes his father's own words: you know my wife bore me two sons; one went out from me, and I said, surely he is torn in pieces, and I haven't seen him since. If you take this one too, and harm comes to him, you'll bring my gray hairs down with sorrow to the grave. Listen to what Judah is doing. He's saying out loud that their father has a favorite, and accepting it. The old jealousy is nowhere to be heard. He tells how he made himself surety for the boy, promising to bring him home. Then the offer: "let thy servant, I pray thee, abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." Take me instead. I'll be your slave for the rest of my life. And the last line: "For how shall I go up to my father, if the lad be not with me?" Think about who's hearing this. Joseph. The brother who was sold into slavery listens as the brother who said sell him offers to become a slave, so that a brother, and a father, won't suffer what Joseph and Jacob suffered. First with Tamar, and now here, Judah is the brother who owns what he did, and then does better.

74.title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
74.hook: he weeps so loudly Egypt hears; "it was not you that sent me hither, but God"
74.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads Joseph's words as a model of forgiveness that names the wrong honestly, and Jewish teachers also stress that forgiving does not require pretending a harm was good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah's plea: the brother who said sell him offered to be a slave so Benjamin could go home. Your line was take me instead.

Judah finishes speaking, and the room goes quiet. The governor can't hold it anymore. Everyone out! he shouts at his servants. Clear the room! The Egyptian guards and attendants file out, and the door closes on eleven frightened Hebrew shepherds and one Egyptian lord. Then he starts crying. Not quietly. He weeps so loudly that the Egyptians outside hear it, and word reaches Pharaoh's house. The brothers have no idea what's happening. They think they're about to be enslaved.
screen: `EVERYONE OUT!` → `HE WEEPS SO LOUD EGYPT HEARS.` → `THE BROTHERS DON'T UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Then, in Hebrew, with no interpreter now: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" Ani Yosef. The brothers can't answer; the text says they were terrified at his presence. The rabbis noticed that silence. One old teacher said: if the brothers couldn't answer Joseph when he spoke one sentence, how will any of us answer on the day we're shown our whole lives? Joseph sees their fear. Come near to me, please, he says, and they come near. I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. He says it. He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. Then: don't be grieved, and don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to preserve life. Two years of famine, five more to come, and I'm here to keep you alive. And the line the whole story has been building to: "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." What is Joseph doing? Readers honestly disagree. Some hear real forgiveness: he's found meaning in his suffering, and he frees his brothers from its weight. Others notice he's reframing it for himself, that he needed this story to survive. And the Torah doesn't say the brothers were off the hook; years later, they're still afraid of him. What the text does show is a man looking back over the pit, the slavery and the prison, and seeing a path. Not a good thing. A road that led somewhere. Then he kisses all his brothers and weeps on them. "And after that his brethren talked with him." For the first time since the coat.

75.title: Blessing the grandsons (Genesis 48)
75.hook: Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, whose names parents still use to bless children on Friday night
75.howItsDone: On Friday night, in homes that keep the custom, parents place their hands on their children's heads and bless them, sons with the names of Ephraim and Manasseh and daughters with Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing from Numbers 6.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ani Yosef: two words, a flood of tears, and a hard road seen as a path. Your line was it led somewhere. Since then, Jacob has come down to Egypt and held his lost son again. Now he's old.

Friday night, in Jewish homes that keep the custom, something happens right before dinner. The candles are lit, the table's set. A parent puts their hands on a child's head, sometimes a squirming toddler, sometimes a teenager rolling their eyes, sometimes a grown child home for the weekend, and says a blessing. For a son, it starts with two names that may surprise you. Not Abraham. Not Moses. Two boys born in Egypt.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, BEFORE DINNER.` → `HANDS ON A CHILD'S HEAD.` → `TWO NAMES FROM EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Jacob is sick, near the end, his eyes dim. Joseph brings his two sons to him, Manasseh the older and Ephraim the younger. And the old man says something that sums up his whole life: "I had not thought to see thy face; and, lo, God hath let me see thy seed also." He thought Joseph was dead, torn by a wild animal. Now he's holding his grandchildren. Joseph places them carefully: the older at Jacob's right hand, the younger at his left. Jacob crosses his arms. Right hand on the younger, Ephraim; left on the older. Joseph tries to fix it. Jacob refuses: I know, my son, I know. The younger will be greater. It's the old pattern of Genesis, younger before older, Jacob before Esau. But this time there's no stolen blessing, no fight. Manasseh doesn't storm off. Then Jacob says: "By thee shall Israel bless, saying: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And that's what Jewish parents who keep the custom still say. Why these two? Commentators give different answers. Some say they're the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight each other. Others say they were born and raised in Egypt, far from home, and still stayed who they were. For daughters, parents name the four mothers: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. Then, for all of them, the old priestly blessing: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."

76.title: Genesis ends (Genesis 49–50)
76.hook: Jacob's blessings, Joseph's forgiveness, and a coffin waiting to go home; finishing a book, the synagogue says "be strong"
76.tomorrow: a king who knew not Joseph
76.howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation stands and calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephraim: Jacob's crossed hands, and a blessing parents still say on Friday night. Your line was may you be like them. Today, the last page of the first book.

A synagogue on a Saturday morning in winter. The Torah scroll lies open on the table, and the reader is chanting the very last verse of Genesis. The whole book, from let there be light to here, is about to be finished. The moment the last word is sung, the whole room stands and calls out together, three words, loud: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. It's a little like the cheer at the end of a long race.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF GENESIS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.`

segments.voice: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses them one by one. The blessings are honest: some praise, some hard words about old wrongs. He asks to be buried with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah, in Canaan, and he dies. Joseph and his brothers carry him home with a great Egyptian procession and bury him. Then, walking back to Egypt, the brothers get scared. Now that Father is gone, maybe Joseph will pay us back. They send him a message, and they fall down before him. Joseph weeps, and says: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God? And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He'll take care of them, and their little ones. Years of peace after the reunion, and they still needed to hear it again. Sometimes forgiveness has to be said twice. Then Joseph grows old, and asks one thing: when God brings you out of here, carry my bones with you. And Genesis ends with this line: "and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." The book that began with a garden ends with a coffin in a foreign land, waiting to go home. That's where chazak comes in. It means be strong. The tradition says it at the end of every one of the five books of the Torah, and it fits here most of all. Something long is finished. The ending isn't tidy. And the next book begins in slavery. So before you turn the page: be strong, be strong, and strengthen each other.

77.title: A king who knew not Joseph (Exodus 1:8–14)
77.hook: a new Pharaoh, fear of a growing people, and slavery
77.howItsDone: The book of Exodus, Shemot in Hebrew, begins its synagogue reading each winter, and its story of slavery and freedom is retold at the Passover seder every spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak: Genesis ended with a coffin in Egypt, and the whole room saying be strong. Your line was be strong, be strong. This week ran from brothers bowing for bread, through the cup, Judah's plea and Ani Yosef, to the end of a book. Today, a new one opens.

The second book of the Torah opens with a list of names: Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt, seventy people. That's why it's called Shemot, Names. Then Joseph dies, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. Their children have children, and the text piles up the words: they were fruitful, they swarmed, they multiplied, they grew very strong, and the land was filled with them. A family has become a people. Then one short verse turns everything: "Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph."
screen: `SHEMOT: NAMES.` → `SEVENTY BECOME A PEOPLE.` → `A NEW KING OVER EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Who knew not Joseph. How could a Pharaoh not know the man who saved Egypt from famine? The Talmud records two answers. One rabbi says it really was a new king. The other says it was the same king, who made new decrees, and acted as if he'd never known Joseph. Forgetting on purpose. Then listen to his speech. The children of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. "Come, let us deal wisely with them," in case there's a war, and they join our enemies. Nobody has done anything. There's no crime, no rebellion. Only a number, and a fear of what that number might do someday. From fear comes a plan: taskmasters and forced labor, building the store cities of Pithom and Raamses. Then the Torah says something almost defiant: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied." The Egyptians came to dread them, so the labor gets harder: mortar, brick, work in the fields, all of it made bitter. This is how the story of the Exodus begins. Not with a monster. With a man who forgot what someone had done for his country, looked at a group of neighbors, and saw a threat. Jews retell this story every year at the Passover seder, and some teachers point out how ordinary its first step is. Forgetting. Then fear. Then cruelty that feels, to the people doing it, like being wise.
screen: `A NEW KING, OR ONE WHO CHOSE TO FORGET?` · `TOO MANY AND TOO MIGHTY FOR US.` · `LET US DEAL WISELY WITH THEM.` · `THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED, THE MORE THEY GREW.` · then, large: `FEAR FORGETS.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time you heard a group of people talked about as a threat: too many of them, they'll take over. Maybe it was on the news; maybe you've thought it. Ask what the fear was based on, something they did or something someone imagined they might do, and just see the first step.
